e-7118.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
e-7118.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in\left[0,1\right].$
e-7118.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

e-9517.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
e-9517.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in[0,\pi]?$
e-9517.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx+1xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=1ti+tj for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫13t−1tdt
b
∫132tdt
c
∫13t2+1tdt
d
2∫131tdt
e
∫13t2−1tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=1t,y(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(1t)i+ddt(t)j=−1t2i+j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxy2dx+1xdy=∫13xy2dxdtdt+1xdydtdt=∫13(xy2dxdt+1xdydt)dt=∫131t⋅t2⋅(−1t2)+1(1t)⋅1dt=∫13−1t+tdt=∫13t2−1tdt

content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t−2)i+(t3−t)j for t∈[1,2]?

a
∫12t(4t2−1)dt
b
∫124t3−3t−2dt
c
∫124t3+t−2dt
d
∫124t3−t−2dt
e
∫124t3−2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x=t-2, y=t³-t, x'=1, and y'=3t²-1. The integrand becomes (x+y)x'+(x+2)y'=(t³-2)+t(3t²-1)=4t³-t-2. Therefore option d is equivalent.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t-2)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j$ for $t\in [1,2]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t−2)i+(t3−t)j for t∈[1,2]?

a
∫12t(4t2−1)dt
b
∫124t3−3t−2dt
c
∫124t3+t−2dt
d
∫124t3−t−2dt
e
∫124t3−2dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t−2,y(t)=t3−t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(t3−t)j=i+(3t2−1)j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy=∫12(x+y)dxdtdt+(x+2)dydtdt=∫12((x+y)dxdt+(x+2)dydt)dt=∫12(t−2+t3−t)⋅1+(t−2+2)⋅(3t2−1)dt=∫12t3−2+3t3−tdt=∫124t3−t−2dt

verification.explanation: Substituting x=t-2, y=t³-t, dx=dt, and dy=(3t²-1)dt gives (t³-2)+t(3t²-1)=4t³-t-2. This confirms option d and agrees with the revealed worked solution; the displayed incorrect submission selected b.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t-2)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j$ for $t\in [1,2]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: With x=t+1, y=-2t², x'=1, and y'=-4t, the integrand is (t+1+4t²)-4t(t+1)=1-3t, giving a directly. Options b and e also have the same integral value, 2, because their odd terms integrate to zero on [-1,1].

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t+1)\,i-2{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t+1,\,y(t)=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+(-4t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$

content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t+1,\,y(t)=-2{t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+(-4t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-2y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(x-2y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}((x-2y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(t+1-2\cdot (-2{t}^{2}))\cdot 1+(t+1)\cdot (-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}t+1+4{t}^{2}-4{t}^{2}-4t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}1-3t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=2sin⁡ti−2cos⁡tj for t∈[0,π2]?

a
2∫0π/2dt
b
4∫0π/2dt
c
2∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
d
4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/22cos⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x=2sin(t), y=-2cos(t), x'=2cos(t), and y'=2sin(t). Thus (x-y)x'+(y-x)y'=4(sin(t)+cos(t))(cos(t)-sin(t))=4cos(2t), giving option d directly. Option c also has the same integral value, zero.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
after.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

a
2∫0π/2dt
b
4∫0π/2dt
c
2∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
d
4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/22cos⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=2sin⁡t,y(t)=−2cos⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2sin⁡t)i+ddt(−2cos⁡t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy=∫0π/2(x−y)dxdtdt+(y−x)dydtdt=∫0π/2((x−y)dxdt+(y−x)dydt)dt=∫0π/2(2sin⁡t−(−2cos⁡t))⋅2cos⁡t+(−2cos⁡t−2sin⁡t)⋅2sin⁡tdt=∫0π/24sin⁡tcos⁡t+4cos2⁡t−4cos⁡tsin⁡t−4sin2⁡tdt=∫0π/24(cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t)dt=∫0π/24cos⁡(2t)dt=4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt

content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]?$
content.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{t},\,y(t)={e}^{t+1}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t+1})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\cdot {e}^{t}+{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{3t+1}+{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
